This pairing is robust and unaffected by interactions that break lattice symmetries, but is instead influenced by a band-resonance interaction that enhances pairing when the chemical potential is near a band's edge. Our work also predicts that superconducting pairing will dominate a topological insulator when interactions are strong, resulting in a $p$-wave superconductor rather than a gapped topological insulator.

The theorem originally stated by Polya concerned the number of ways to divide a set with n elements into k non-empty parts. We've extended this to groups of sets whose elements are 1-dimensional connected locally compact Abelian groups.

In the analysis of presence-absence data, a clustering method is often applied to group species assemblages with similar composition. Several clustering methods have been proposed for such data, including those based on matrix factorization, random forests, and dissimilarity matrices. This study evaluates the effectiveness of these approaches using simulated data under varying conditions and recommends a method that performs well in high-dimensional environments.

This paper presents a novel, efficient method for salient object detection that utilizes RGB and RGB-D data. The proposed framework, U4D, integrates four distinct components: a self-similarity structure, a cross-modal interaction module, a depth-embedded attention mechanism, and a cross-modal fusion module. The self-similarity structure and cross-modal interaction module effectively leverage data characteristics to extract high-level features from RGB and RGB-D data. The depth-embedded attention mechanism selectively emphasizes relevant information from RGB and depth features to generate preliminary saliency maps. The cross-modal fusion module fuses the maps using a weighted average to produce the final output. The framework's design enables it to be applied to both RGB and RGB-D datasets, thus enhancing its versatility. The method's efficiency stems from its ability to process information in a unified manner, thereby reducing computational complexity. The proposed framework outperforms existing methods in saliency prediction and depth-assisted performance on the MSRA-YaleB, NUS-3D, and PASCAL-Seg datasets.

This paper details our approach to the 2019 SemEval Task 6, focusing on identifying aggressive language in Spanish and English. Our UM-IU@LING system combined BERT and SVM models to predict the levels of aggression in given tweets. Our results showed strong performance in subtask A2 (Spanish) and subtask A1 (English), with our SVM-based approach achieving 0.7964 and 0.7947 macro-averaged F1 scores respectively.

The set of two-digit palindromic numbers is examined in detail, particularly with regard to their quotients by one-digit numbers. It's demonstrated that the set of all possible two-digit numbers can be precisely divided into three distinct parts, based on the quotients they share with one-digit numbers. The first of these parts comprises the set of two-digit palindromic numbers, while the other two parts consist of a specific subset of two-digit non-palindromic numbers with unique characteristics.

This study introduces a non-convex variational framework to reconstruct CT images while considering multiple energy levels, removing noise from X-ray sensors, and identifying distinct materials. The framework uses variational regularization to address these challenges, which are then tackled through an iterative alternating minimization approach. The results of our experiments using simulated data show the efficacy of our proposed method in material decomposition and noise reduction, outperforming a convex formulation and reference algorithms.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) in developing countries is a challenging task due to limited resources, making it difficult to achieve good results. A specific problem in Nigeria involves recognizing handwritten Oluwasegun, a Yoruba-based language. The key obstacles in solving this problem include a small dataset and the complexity of Oluwasegun, which has distinct characteristics from standard Yoruba. To overcome these challenges, we developed a new approach for creating synthetic datasets from a single image. The method enables the production of diverse written texts, which can be used to augment existing datasets and improve model performance. The results of our experiments using this approach on Oluwasegun HTR showed a significant improvement of 6.5% in character error rate compared to a baseline model.

Merging ab initio calculations of heavy nuclei is a complex task due to their large size. Calculations using the South Carolina ab initio model with 12 neutrons and 12 protons demonstrate the difficulties involved. These calculations require significant computational resources, leading to a 4096-core calculation that still falls short of convergence. Various method limitations, such as the 0-range approximation and the Hartree-Fock approximation, also contribute to the challenges. These issues highlight the need for more advanced computational techniques and larger-scale parallel processing.

This educational review offers a thorough examination of the SSH model, a quantum system that exhibits topological properties. It provides a detailed analysis of the SSH model's concepts, including its wave functions, energy spectrum, and the ideas behind topological insulators. The review also delves into the SSH model's various approximations and extensions, showcasing the diversity of concepts linked to the system.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with bounded convex domains in higher-dimensional complex spaces. It is demonstrated that for a function to create a compact composition operator, it must be restricted to a specific set of mappings. Furthermore, an alternate characterization of this restriction is provided in the context of one-dimensional complex spaces, and it is also shown that an additional constraint is necessary if the domain is not convex. The investigation is extended to Bergman spaces of analytic discs within polynomially bounded regions of one-dimensional complex spaces.

We have calculated the two-loop amplitude for the graviton scattering in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using two different methods. One method involved direct computation using the AdS/CFT correspondence, while the other involved reducing a higher-dimensional amplitude to three-point functions of gauge field operators in four-dimensional space-time, which are then related to each other via the AdS/CFT correspondence.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a high-performance, parallel memory allocator designed for use in object-based programming on GPUs. The memory management component is a significant obstacle to overcome when developing efficient GPU code, particularly when dealing with dynamic memory allocation. Our proposed allocator is based on a novel strategy that uses a direct memory access approach and a hierarchical tree structure to efficiently manage memory allocation and deallocation operations on GPUs. The performance of DynaSOAr is evaluated and compared to a widely used, high-performance memory allocator on a variety of workloads, resulting in significant speedup and memory access efficiency improvements.

We investigate a $U(1)_X$ model derived from the $SO(10)$ completion with a single extra gauge fermion. The fermion and fermion-Higgs sectors in two different cases are examined, followed by a detailed analysis of the fermion-Higgs vertex corrections within the one-loop level. Furthermore, we explore the implications of the $Z_2$ symmetry on the kinetic term mixing and the Majorana mass for the right-handed neutrinos, before discussing the potential extra gauge fermion signatures at the LHC.

The mechanics of a hollow, cylindrical structure subjected to uniaxial tension and internal pressure are examined. Analytical expressions for the stress and strain states in terms of the material properties, radius, and length of the cylinder are derived. A parametric study is then conducted to investigate how the stress and strain states are influenced by the internal pressure and longitudinal tension. Additionally, the findings are applied to analyze the mechanical stability of a hollow cylinder, such as a cane tube, which is a component of a bicycle frame.

Incorporating uncertainty into complex systems is crucial for making reliable decisions, which can be achieved through Bayesian network models that incorporate sets of possible probability distributions. However, ensuring the reliability of measures taken based on these models requires analyzing the worst-case scenarios of their probabilistic inferences. This paper presents a method to provide assurances for reliable inference in Bayesian networks with uncertain probability distributions represented as sets of possible probabilistic circuits. The approach involves reducing the problem of finding the minimum and maximum inferences into a more manageable form and provides efficient algorithms to analyze the bounds of inferences reliably under worst-case scenarios.

This research demonstrates the occurrence of Bloch oscillations in ultrasonic wave propagation. By using a 2D plate with a periodic pattern of holes, created through a laser-based micromachining technique, we generate a Wannier-Stutzmann-like model. This model reveals a Wannier-Stutzmann singularity at the Brillouin zone boundary in the phase space. In the time domain, we observe Bloch oscillations characterized by a gradual shift in the time-dependent phase of ultrasonic waves over time, as modulated by an external acoustic wave.

A partial spread system in a generalised quadrangle is defined by a set of incident vertex-line pairs that cannot belong to the same block. We investigate the relationship between partial spreads and a specific type of code, known as a neighbor-transitive code, within the framework of a generalized quadrangle. We establish that a neighbor-transitive code in a generalized quadrangle gives rise to a partial spread, and provide an example of a code that corresponds to a non-existent partial spread in the classical quadrangle. We also examine the code's properties in the case of a classical quadrangle and a grid graph.

The Central Molecular Zone in the Milky Way is a unique region with distinct star formation patterns and anisotropic density distributions. To better understand this area, we applied a two-dimensional correlation function to analyze the density structure of the Central Molecular Zone. The analysis revealed that the region's density patterns are influenced by anisotropic distributions, with the most significant distortions at high-density areas. The findings are consistent with previous research and provide further insight into the Central Molecular Zone's complex density structure.

The X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (XANES) is a powerful tool for examining the local structure of materials, particularly in their unoccupied electronic states. The application of XANES to materials undergoing a phase transition at high fluence is limited by the non-linear response it elicits. To overcome this, a rate model is developed that accounts for the increasing density of electron groups as X-ray fluence rises, enabling the non-linear XANES signal to be isolated. The model is validated by comparing its output to detailed density functional theory calculations of a model system, with the results indicating that the rate model can accurately predict the non-linear XANES signal at high fluences.

A low-power temperature sensor, suitable for IoT applications, has been designed with a total area of 0.045mm$^2$ and is built using a standard 0.13$\mu$m CMOS process. The sensor uses a single-ended bipolar transconductor amplifier and a Gm-boost converter to achieve a large temperature resolution of 0.24$\deg$C and a relatively small error margin of $\pm$1.4$\deg$C within 0 to 100$\deg$C. The sensor's analog-to-digital conversion process consumes only 1.06nJ per conversion and operates at a clock frequency of 1.8MHz, with a conversion time of 0.56$\mu$s.

Heralded entanglement swapping without the need for post-selection is a crucial technique for generating entangled photons on a large scale. This method, however, is often limited by the post-selection process itself, especially when dealing with polarization entanglement. This study introduces a new approach, leveraging quantum scissors to create polarization entanglement in a single step. By utilizing a quantum scissor metamaterial, we demonstrate the simultaneous generation of two entangled photons with orthogonal polarizations, achieving a high entanglement fidelity of 0.983 and a high single-photon visibility of 0.983 as well.

A digital geometric structure is created by imposing geometric constraints on a digital environment, similar to how traditional geometric structures are constrained. This research focuses on developing digital Euclidean spanners for certain geometric spaces, such as points and line segments in a grid, under various metrics. The study introduces digital Euclidean spanners for shortest paths and Dijkstra's algorithms in a grid-based metric. It also shows that any digital Euclidean spanner for a line segment metric cannot be approximated within a factor better than Ω(log n) unless P=NP.

In IoT environments, data from sensors generates an enormous amount of information, 
making it crucial to use feature extraction techniques to streamline this process.
However, these models often overlook the distinct characteristics of sensors, 
resulting in poor performance. This study addresses this issue by developing an 
efficient feature selection algorithm tailored to multi-feature, single-class IoT 
sensors, with a focus on cost-sensitivity to handle imbalanced data sets. 
Experimental results using real-world data from UCI and IoT domains validate the 
model's effectiveness.

Godel modal logic encompasses a family of modal logics characterized by the (4) axiom, which can be modelled through relational structures featuring a binary accessibility relation accessible by formulae. This class also includes Godel's original modal logic as well as its extension with the (K) axiom, known as S2. By introducing a specific algebraic framework, the finite representability of Godel modal logic can be established. This result is further generalized to obtain finite representability for certain extensions of Godel modal logic, including those with the (K) or (4) axioms.

This paper investigates the feasibility of creating word alignments between two languages in real-time, utilizing data from multiple external bilingual sources. Word alignment is a crucial task in various Machine Translation (MT) and Translation Studies applications. While significant progress has been made in using aligned corpora, they are often scarce in areas of low-demand, high-demand areas like translating social media posts into a different language. We can leverage a large amount of non-aligned bilingual text from social media by relying on bilingual dictionaries or word pairs. This paper demonstrates how to create word alignments on-the-fly using such dictionaries and shows that the resulting alignments are effective in MT applications, even outperforming high-quality, fully-annotated corpora in some cases.

The distorted resolvent algorithm is an iterative method for finding Nash equilibria in various games by leveraging monotone and Lipschitz continuous correspondences. It offers a versatile solution that can be applied to a broad class of Nash equilibrium problems with considerable computational efficiency. The algorithm's implementation is relatively straightforward and enables the construction of Nash equilibria for a wide range of games, including those with large dimensions and infinite players, at a low computational cost.

We introduce PopSyCLE, a Python tool for calculating the mass function of primordial black holes that can account for dark matter. This code enables the integration of multiple PBH mass functions, allowing for a more accurate representation of potential sources of dark matter. A demonstration of its capabilities is shown through the implementation of two variants: one based on Gaussian fluctuations and another that incorporates N-body merger tree calculations. The latter model can be used to investigate the effects of tidal disruption on PBH mass functions. Furthermore, we utilize PopSyCLE to analyze a model in which a portion of dark matter is composed of a low-mass black hole sub-structure. This model is capable of explaining the observed Galactic Centre excess in the GeV energy range without conflicting with constraints from the Fermi-LAT satellite.

In a system of hard wedges composed of spheres with a specific wedge angle, we investigate the emergence of liquid crystalline phases with splay modulations. Our findings reveal that these modulations are confined to certain wedge angles where the 2D hexatic phase and the phase with nematic splay do not occur. We present phase diagrams for two different types of splay modulations and explain how their deformed nature arises.

This study introduces novel one-step recurrence relations for stagnant random fields on the sphere, applicable to Gaussian and non-Gaussian base fields. These recurrence relations enable efficient simulation of random fields with covariance characterized by a Mat\'ern function, along with fields with non-Gaussian distributions such as the product of Gaussian and polynomial chaos, incorporating various types of correlation decay. The recurrence relations can be utilized to generate random fields with spatial dependencies on the sphere, reducing the computational time and complexity associated with existing three-step recurrence methods.

We have developed a novel technique for visualizing quantum states using a single pixel by harnessing undetected photons. This method leverages the interaction-free measurement principle, where a quantum state is projected onto a specific basis by interacting with multiple undistinguished photons. We demonstrate the technique's effectiveness with both single and dual undistinguished photons, achieving high fidelity visualizations of arbitrary quantum states, especially in scenarios with high undistinguished photon loss rates or limited resources.

The interaction between liquid liquid interfaces is a long-standing interest in scientific study. When two liquid drops are placed on a soap foam, causing it to get stuck due to surface tension, leading to an increase in the foam's friction. This effect is primarily caused by the increase in the foam's viscosity, which is a result of the creation of a complex liquid network at the drop-drop interface. The frictional force is proportional to the size of the drops and the surface tension of the liquid, while it is independent of the drops' weight. The increase in frictional force is also influenced by the type of liquid used, as well as the presence of surfactants.

In the field of dermatology, identifying and classifying skin lesions is a crucial task for diagnosing various types of skin cancer and other skin conditions. This study presents an advanced deep learning-based framework for classifying skin cancer by utilizing entropy to pinpoint atypical samples. By leveraging entropy, the model distinguishes typical lesions from unusual ones, which are then integrated into the training process to enhance its classification capabilities. This custom approach enables the model to focus on learning characteristic features related to the lesion's morphology rather than its arbitrary shape. This is particularly crucial for detecting rare and specialized skin cancers. Our model's accuracy was evaluated on the ISBI 2017 challenge dataset and showed improved results in rare skin cancer classification compared to standard deep learning methods.

We have calculated the lifetime of quasi-particles in sodium using ab initio many-body calculations. The calculations took into account the influence of long-range electron-electron interactions but also constrained the strong coupling limit. The results revealed that the lifetime of quasi-particles in sodium is on the order of 10^-14 seconds, which is comparable to experimental findings. The study also showed that the leading cause of quasi-particle decay is related to the velocity dispersion of electrons rather than their density.

We present a novel approach to study microcanonical trajectories that maintain a fixed number of particles, energy, and volume. This method overcomes limitations in previous research that relied on canonical ensemble simulations, which are affected by volume changes. We utilize this method to analyze free expansion trajectories in a 2D harmonic potential. The results show that neither energy nor number fluctuations are evenly distributed in this process, contrary to initial predictions. The newly developed method enables the examination of microcanonical dynamics, allowing for a deeper understanding of nonequilibrium processes.

This passage examines the weight calculations of connection and curvature graphs within a finite number of simple Poisson structures. Our analysis employs a novel approach to extend these calculations, initially derived by Berman and Sullivant for a single structure, to the context of multiple Poisson structures. Specifically, we generalize their findings to a scenario involving k Poisson structures, each defined on a d-dimensional oriented hypergraph domain. Our generalization yields an explicit formula for the curvature graph weights in terms of a sum over hyperedges, along with a separate formula for the connection graph weights. These formulas demonstrate that the curvature graph weights are a function of the hyperedge weights, exclusively, while the connection graph weights also depend on the initial and final points of the edges.

We investigate the propagation of solitary waves in a pre-stressed timber-like chain with equally spaced masses and nonlinear interconnections. The analysis reveals that these solitary waves can only occur when the system's stiffness is below a specific threshold, determined by the geometric arrangement. Furthermore, we show that two solitary waves with opposite directions will not pass through each other in a conservative system, indicating their localized nature. The study also considers a timber-like chain with mass asymmetry and finds that solitary waves still exist within a specific range of stiffness, although their behavior differs from that in asymmetric granular chains.

During the inflationary era, the cosmos can give rise to tiny, primordial particles known as cosmological collider particles. These particles are produced through the collision of standard model fields' fluctuations, which are separated by the scale of inflation. As a result, the cosmic landscape contains distinct "resonance peaks" characterized by specific masses. This study explores classical effects of these cosmological collider particles, which are generated simultaneously with their quantum counterparts. It is demonstrated that the quantum and classical versions of these particles are strongly correlated, particularly in environments lacking symmetry, where the quantum particle's properties are defined by specific "kink" states. Moreover, the quantum and classical particles exhibit distinct features in specific symmetry-breaking scenarios, which are influenced by the rate of inflation and field velocities.

A graph is classified as an accordion graph if it can be constructed by merging the 2-factor of a quartic circulant graph along a Hamiltonian cycle that encompasses all the outer vertices. It is demonstrated in this study that an accordion graph either possesses a unique quartic circulant representation or is isomorphic to another quartic circulant graph. The investigation also shows that an accordion graph features a Hamiltonian 2-factor characterized by a cycle that includes all its outer vertices, as well as a perfect matching that can be derived from a perfect matching in its quartic circulant equivalent, if it exists.

We investigate one-dimensional quantum walks with three possible states in a periodic structure, considering various initial conditions and non-uniform coin operator configurations. Our analysis focuses on the probability distribution's spread, leading to the definition of a characteristic path. By examining the system's dynamics, we develop scaling laws that apply globally in space and time, influenced by the coin operator's non-diagonal elements and initial state distribution. These scaling laws are validated numerically and are unaffected by the specific coin operator's form.

Vision transformers have shown remarkable performance in computer vision tasks, but their application in unsupervised learning has been limited by the complexity of existing self-supervised learning methods. In contrast, we demonstrate that a simple method, like distillation with linear projections, can unlock the potential of vision transformers for unsupervised learning. Furthermore, we observe that the emerging features in this approach have a distinct characteristic - they are edge-related. This property enables our model to excel in low-data scenarios and perform well on tasks like semantic segmentation, even without supervision.

We suggest a novel dual dark matter and dark energy model based on a modified Cardassos energy density function, with a repulsive force dominating at large distances and a stronger dissipation effect in the dark matter sector than in the dark energy sector when the distance is short. We then investigate the properties of the cosmological constant of this model, including its stability and the conditions under which it becomes spontaneous. We also examine the model's parameter space, focusing on the relationship between the effective dissipation coefficient and the mass gap, as well as the impact of dissipation on the phase transition. We finally verify that this model is consistent with current cosmological observations by analyzing the model's equation of state and spectral index.

We present a simple proof that the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically using Sobolev spaces with high smoothness and certain types of Lorentz spaces with smoothness.

This paper introduces a stable version of the latent diffusion creator, which produces high-quality images by interacting with a semantic guide in the diffusion model's stable state. The guide, represented as a neural creator, can be learned to produce consistent outputs and is adjustable on a continuum from unconditional to conditional creators. The system's consistent nature enables the creation of multiple images without compromising the model's stability. The research demonstrates that the stable creator excels at generating images accompanied by semantic descriptions, achieving superior results compared to the unstable version and state-of-the-art diffusion-based and GAN-based methods on the CUB dataset.

This research introduces a novel method for concealing image data by modifying pixels in an invertible manner. A specific type of neural network, called a Bayesian Neural Network, is utilized to create an invertible function that can be applied to pixel values, resulting in a predictable shift. Subsequently, an image filtering technique is employed to create an effective masking method that can be reversed by utilizing the network's parameters as additional input data. This approach is demonstrated to provide a strong steganographic method that can withstand various statistical analysis attacks.

The $J/\psi$ decaying into invisible particles offers an attractive approach to understanding the properties of neutrinos and dark matter. By analyzing the branching ratio of this process, we can derive significant limitations on the low-energy parameters of neutrino and dark matter effective field theories. These limitations are particularly stringent when the dark matter particle weighs less than the $J/\psi$ particle.

The presence of magnetic bright points in the solar atmosphere is a strong indication of the impact of magnetic fields on the solar surface. To better understand these features, we analyzed data from the GONG g-band filtergraph project, which provided us with time series measurements of magnetic bright points. This analysis revealed that the distribution of their sizes and durations could be accurately represented by a combination of two Gaussian functions. This finding is supported by previous research on the subject and has significant implications for modeling these phenomena.

Human vision efficiently identifies and tracks moving objects, enabling us to perceive a stable environment despite significant background motion. This is crucial for everyday vision and has been replicated in computer algorithms, but the underlying human process is still not fully understood. By analyzing minimal human films, which show a person moving while a camera remains stationary, we investigate whether these films contain sufficient information for a stable visual perception. We examine the relationship between camera movements, which are restricted to pan and tilt, and the resulting human behavior. These minimal films lead to novel insights into the relationship between object recognition and eye movement, revealing that a stable visual perception depends on detecting and tracking specific patterns within the film sequence.

Dark matter composed of magnetic monopoles, fueled by an anomaly that cancels charge, offers an explanation for the universe's non-zero magnetic flux. This theory is most plausible when dark matter consists of monopoles with very small magnetic charges, on the order of $10^{-18}$ elementary charges. In this scenario, dark matter's ability to resist being captured by galaxies would be maintained, thus preserving their magnetic fields. This model is compatible with current limits set by laboratory direct detection experiments and cosmic microwave background observations.

Predicting the future is a complex task in weather forecasting. To address this, a new deep learning model is proposed that uses a novel transformer framework with a shifted window cross-attention mechanism, enabling it to effectively predict the future states of weather datasets. The proposed framework consists of two main components: a shifted window cross-attention module and a multi-scale hierarchical encoder. The first component enables the model to focus on similar areas in different times and encode long-term dependencies, while the second component captures local details and long-term information at multiple scales. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through experiments on real-world weather datasets, achieving a significant improvement over state-of-the-art models.

In models featuring three Higgs doublets, a broken $S_3$ symmetry can lead to at most one Higgs doublet being involved in fermion interactions, while the other two are either not coupled or couple to fermions in an opposite manner. We investigate a specific class of $S_3$-extended three Higgs doublet models where a dark matter candidate can be either a Higgs-like or a light scalar. When a Higgs-like scalar acts as dark matter, it is possible to achieve compatibility with electroweak precision data by introducing an extra $S_3$-breaking term. For the scenario where a light scalar acts as dark matter, we find that the model can be made $Z_2$-invariant, resulting in a fully natural model where dark matter is light. Furthermore, we identify a potential advantage of this $S_3$-extended three Higgs doublet model over the inert doublet model in the context of dark matter direct detection.

A fundamental conjecture in quantum mechanics, known as the PPT conjecture, suggests that certain properties of matrices imply their non-positive definiteness. While this conjecture holds for most cases, there is one exception where it does not - the quadrilateral conjecture. We have found that the quadrilateral conjecture is true in a specific subset of situations, specifically when the matrices in question are positive semi-definite.

In neurons, the balance of ions and nutrients relies heavily on a complex system that involves the regulation of transport mechanisms and pathways. To simulate this process, we developed a mathematical model that accounts for the biophysical properties of various substances being transported across cell membranes. The model includes a nonlinear optimization component to ensure that transport mechanisms operate efficiently and effectively. The study focuses on a two-dimensional model of a neuron with a compact cell body and a single axon, bounded by a membrane with multiple transport mechanisms. The model requires an optimal control problem to be solved, which is based on partial differential equations and is challenging to solve numerically.

Understanding complex financial time series data is crucial for informing investment decisions.
Network analysis provides a valuable framework for exploring and interpreting relationships between time series, 
especially in detecting hidden patterns and common connections.
This study introduces a novel method for identifying recurring patterns or relationships in large financial network datasets, 
which is particularly effective given its ability to handle large datasets and accommodate diverse time series interlinkages.
The proposed algorithm is tested on real-world datasets and its performance is evaluated using various metrics.

In a binary system containing a white dwarf and a black hole, we examine the interaction between the white dwarf and the point mass representing the black hole using the Newtonian approximation. As the white dwarf approaches the black hole, its material begins to emit radiation, which is studied across various phases of the approach. Initially, the white dwarf's outer layers are heated by gravitational forces, causing them to emit thermal radiation. As the star draws closer, its inner core heats up due to gravitational collapse, leading to the emission of non-thermal radiation. As the white dwarf crosses the Roche lobe, mass from its outer layers is transferred to the inner core, where it accumulates and eventually forms an accretion disk. This process is accompanied by the emission of viscous energy from the disk. Our findings align with existing research and provide a comprehensive picture of the white dwarf's energy emission across its approach to the black hole.

In a study on three-body $\tau$-lepton decays involving hadrons, various scenarios are examined where the virtual W boson interacts with the $\tau$-lepton via vector or axial-vector currents. Calculations are performed using three different approaches: one with weak interactions applied to individual particles acting independently, another using a hadronic system in its ground state, and a method for describing the hadronic system through form factors. The examination of three-body decay distributions in this study serves to illustrate the distinct characteristics of different current structures.

We establish a connection between the Tversky distance and the normalized information distance, with the latter being a modification of the Levenshtein distance. The Tversky distance is a measure of dissimilarity between two sets, with its value ranging from 0 to 1, whereas its analog, the normalized information distance, takes values within the interval [0, 1 ∪ 0, 1], with the latter being a measure of similarity. The relationship between these two distances is defined by a family of parametric functions, with one parameter determining the asymptotic behavior of the function and the other influencing its curvature.

A novel approach to motion deblurring is presented, which leverages a network trained on blurred images to counteract real-world blurring effects. The proposed method relies on a self-supervised learning technique that employs synthetic blur information to differentiate between blurring caused by moving objects and that caused by the viewer. The pseudo-blur synthesizer, a key component of the method, generates the blurring factor by transforming the scene and object motion maps into a spatial blur matrix. The efficiency of this method is demonstrated through successful application to blurry images, as well as comparison with existing motion deblurring techniques in the linear domain.

To explore the potential of DNA-based computational systems, we've developed a project where a group of DNA molecules, organized into a network, mimic a basic spiking neuron's learning process, similar to Hebbian learning. This DNA network, made up of different DNA molecules, is designed to interact with each other in a specific way, representing the connections between neurons. By applying a pre-defined learning rule, the DNA molecules are programmed to change their interactions based on past "spikes," leading to increased connection strength between those molecules that have "spiked" together. This results in a system that can learn and remember patterns of DNA molecule interactions.

This paper delves into the properties of interval chains within the ultrapowers of ordered sets. It first presents a method to construct the interval chains in $\mathbb{R}$-ultrapowers, demonstrating their equivalence to $\kappa$-many continuous real functions. Next, it is proven that for a non-compact ordered set, its $\mathbb{R}$-ultrapower is complete if and only if it contains a scale similar to those found in $\omega$-ultrapowers of countable ordered sets. Additionally, it is shown that the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$-ultrapowers is independent of the cardinality of the index set used for ultrapower construction.

Deep learning model training is now a common activity, but the process can be
involving due to the large size of datasets. To streamline this process, a
pre-training step is often used to reduce the time required for model
training. However, current pre-training methods are not tailored to specific
datasets and are instead based on general characteristics. To improve this process,
we propose a new method that involves analyzing datasets on an individual basis
to optimize the pre-training step. This method involves identifying key factors
that affect model convergence and creating a customized pre-training routine
based on these factors. Our research shows that this method can lead to a
substantial reduction in model training time, often by 50% or more, when
compared to traditional methods.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture suggests that every graph with n or more vertices, colored with t or more different colors, must necessarily contain a complete subgraph of size t, consisting of at least two vertices. This has been supported by a proof for the specific case of 4-chromatic graphs. Furthermore, a particular class of 5-chromatic graphs, known as Kneser graphs, has also been shown to fulfill the conjecture. This work aims to demonstrate that the Hadwiger's Conjecture holds true for all 4- and 5-chromatic graphs.

Kernel-based methods have gained significant attention in signal processing due to their ability to analyze non-linear patterns. However, these methods are susceptible to outliers, which can compromise their performance. This research introduces an enhanced framework for kernel-based non-linear non-parametric regression, focusing on reconstructing smooth graph signals. The new framework incorporates an adaptive kernel width that ensures optimal results regardless of its choice. The proposed method utilizes the generalized correntropy criterion, derived from kernel-based measures, and is highly resistant to outliers. This is supported by theoretical analysis and substantiated by simulation outcomes.

We've developed a technique utilizing entangled spinor interferometry to generate customized spin states, which can resist and compensate various measurement errors. Our method is demonstrated by creating a specific triaxial state with high precision using nuclear magnetic resonance, and its effectiveness is tested against different types of measurement noise.

We provide exact formulas for the first Robin eigenvalue of a given nonlinear elliptic operator, precise to the second order, under the assumption that the operator in question is uniformly elliptic and its coefficients exhibit smooth dependence on the space.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) efficiently process graph data by convolving neighboring nodes, but the underlying mechanism is complex and difficult to grasp. Researchers have attempted to simplify this by comparing GCNNs to traditional CNNs, but these analogies fall short of providing a clear understanding. This study introduces a new approach that clearly illustrates the basis of GCNNs by drawing a parallel with the matched filtering method from signal processing. Using this analogy, we demonstrate the matched filtering principle and its equivalence to GCNNs, and also derive a new proof for GCNNs' layer-wise feature propagation.

This paper introduces a self-supervised learning method to improve dependency parsing in low-resource scenarios without any enhanced models or additional tasks.
The proposed DCSP method leverages contextualized representations from BERT to generate synthetic dependency parses from raw BERT tree structures.
These synthetic parses are combined with actual parses from high-resource languages to train a parser model, which achieves superior results on low-resource languages with access to BERT models.
Notably, DCSP outperforms a comparable model from the same paradigm by 2.5% UAS and 3.5% LAS on WSJ, and also shows effectiveness on languages without BERT models.

We have performed a detailed analysis within the framework of the light-front quark model to examine the transition form factors of the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ process. The calculated results for the $B\to D$ transition form factors $f_1(Q^2)$, $f_2(Q^2)$, and $f_3(Q^2)$ are consistent with standard model predictions for isospin-violating effects in $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ decay.

We're investigating the connection between non-reversible symmetries and k-differentials in branes. Similar to how a group's action generates cohomology classes, a non-reversible group's action generates cohomology classes of k-differentials. This relationship is particularly evident in the case of D-branes, where these cohomology classes correspond to de Rham cohomology classes of the space where the D-branes are located.

We demonstrate in this paper a comprehensive characterization of all feasible computations that can be carried out through a systematic and methodical approach, utilizing a fixed and predetermined structure. This development is rooted in a fundamental theorem that reveals a profound equivalence between two distinct computational paradigms, one that operates without choice and one that operates symmetrically. This characterization is grounded in an in-depth analysis of a specific type of graph, one that is inherently directed and asymmetric.

We investigated the electronic and orbital characteristics of (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 using hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, revealing that the material undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition within the 0.4 < x < 0.5 doping range. Our results indicate that the Ir 4d-5d gap shrinks as x increases, eventually disappearing at x = 0.5. Additionally, we observed a shift in the Ir 4p core level towards higher binding energies, suggesting increased covalency with x. Our HAXPES data are supported by theoretical band structure calculations, which show that the Ir 4d-5d hybridization decreases with x due to reduced overlap between Ir 5d orbitals on neighboring Eu ions. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the driving force for the insulator-to-metal transition is the suppression of Ir 5d orbital freezing by Bi doping.

This study establishes various existence criteria for a Lipschitz selection of a set-valued mapping defined within a two-dimensional Euclidean space. Several novel iterative algorithms are also proposed to generate such a selection, which demonstrates strong convergence in the presence of certain conditions. These results are further generalized to the case of a Lipschitz multimap defined within a two-dimensional Euclidean space, for which both necessary and sufficient conditions of existence are established.

The Cyclic Monotonicity and Transitivity principles have been widely recognized as effective criteria for model comparison in various fields. However, we demonstrate that applying these principles can lead to adverse consequences in some cases, potentially resulting in the selection of an inferior model over a superior one. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of a nontransitive sufficient decrease in likelihood and establish its relationship with the Cyclic Monotonicity and Transitivity principles. We also provide specific examples to illustrate the implications of this nontransitive property in both Bayesian and frequentist contexts.

Evaluating software system configurations is a labor-intensive process, requiring extensive testing of various setup combinations. This research investigates the potential of reducing setup costs during execution by optimizing setup options earlier, at compile-time. A novel approach is introduced, which identifies and specializes the possible setup spaces for a system based on the results of a prior evaluation, thus minimizing the number of possible setup combinations. A detailed framework is developed to achieve this specialization, along with an empirical analysis of its application to three real-world software systems. The results show that this method can significantly lower the number of possible setup combinations and reduce the time required for a new setup, with the exact savings depending on the specific system and setup options.

Light dark matter particles are readily produced in certain astrophysical environments and can be sensed through their interactions with ordinary matter. A proposed experimental approach involves using high-energy electrons to directly detect sub-GeV dark matter particles, and this method is particularly effective when the target material is heavily bombarded to produce electron excitations. This can be achieved with a small, 1 cm^3 test setup using a thin silicon detector and a beam of 10 GeV protons. This approach offers a viable solution for detecting dark matter particles in a wide range of masses and cross-sections, and could be an attractive option for future dark matter detection experiments.

We investigate the dynamics of a two-level atom interacting with a two-mode cavity in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, where both the atom and cavity modes begin in an entangled state. The analysis focuses on the time-dependent behavior of the atom-cavity entanglement, Rabi oscillations, and cavity transmission, influenced by the atom-cavity coupling strength and initial entanglement. Interestingly, when the atom-cavity coupling is weak, the initial entanglement determines the probability of Rabi oscillations occurring, whereas strong coupling leads to Rabi oscillations being independent of initial conditions. Additionally, we find that the cavity transmission is heavily dependent on the atom-cavity coupling strength and initial conditions, with no transmission observed in the weak coupling regime.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is a critical task for detecting cardiovascular conditions and understanding the heart's functioning. A novel approach using a Tiramisu model is proposed to estimate IBIs from pre-processed ECG signals, where the network's first stage generates feature maps and the second stage performs regression to predict IBIs. This method leverages parallel data streams to extract features and IBIs, where the feature maps are used for further classification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in estimating IBIs and generating relevant features for classification.

Active particle models like the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) represent a simplified form of active matter where a particle's movement is self-driven rather than influenced by random fluctuations. Introducing a non-zero correlation time in these models leads to a particle motion that can be described as a semi-active form of passive Brownian motion. Our study examines the probability distribution of the work done by a semi-active particle over a fixed distance, as well as the time required for the particle to travel a specific distance. Our results reveal that the probability distribution of work is Gaussian in nature, while the first moment of the work distribution is directly proportional to the correlation time and the distance, and has a power-law dependence on the average velocity. Conversely, the second moment of the work distribution is directly proportional to the correlation time, the distance, and the average velocity, but has a different power-law dependence. Furthermore, our results show that the mean time required for the particle to travel a specific distance is directly proportional to the correlation time, the distance, and the average velocity, but has a different power-law dependence.

This study introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset that captures a wide range of human body gestures. It consists of 2,000,000 annotated images from 10 different viewpoints, accompanied by detailed 3D information. HUMBI was created using a novel, efficient method that combines multiple 2D cues to generate precise 3D annotations. Our research showcases the potential of the dataset by achieving remarkable results in 3D human pose estimation and gesture recognition tasks, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. To facilitate further advancements, we propose a benchmark challenge that invites researchers to utilize HUMBI in innovative ways.

We investigate the potential for neural task representations to facilitate model-agnostic, cross-lingual transfer in NLP. By defining a task representation, we can leverage it as weak supervision for low-resource languages. Given that task representations lack explicit structure, we employ clustering and information-theoretic techniques to establish a connection between task representation clusters and linguistic characteristics. Our experiments demonstrate that neural task representations can enable significant improvements in low-resource settings across sentiment analysis and question-answering tasks, with an additional finding of their relationship with linguistic characteristics.

This paper presents BasicVSR++, a video super-resolution model that surpasses current state-of-the-art models like VideoEnhanceNet by a significant margin while requiring significantly fewer parameters - 10.4 MB compared to 198 MB. The improved model is based on a simple and efficient encoder-decoder framework that outperforms VideoEnhanceNet in various evaluations, including PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS loss measures.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single model to learn from multiple environments can lead to catastrophic interference, where previously learned skills are lost as the agent trains in new tasks. To address this issue, we propose a model-based multi-task reinforcement learning approach that uses separate networks for each environment to prevent skill degradation across tasks. While this method avoids catastrophic interference, it can result in underutilization of the agent's knowledge, as each network has limited capacity to learn from experience. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a shared set of abstract action representations that facilitate cross-task sharing of experience, and a novel attention mechanism allowing the agent to selectively learn from experiences relevant to each task. We evaluate our approach through experiments on multi-task grid-worlds and classic control problems, achieving state-of-the-art results and demonstrating the benefits of our method in real-world applications.

We've developed a general method for enhancing the performance of heat engines operating within specific time frames. Our approach allows for a wide range of controls, and we've demonstrated its applicability through two finite-time thermal engineering scenarios, one involving an arbitrary temperature distribution and another with a specific geometric configuration.

This research explores the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems, focusing on the spatial effects of the severe weather. The analysis is conducted using a simulation-based approach that combines a hurricane/storm surge model with a power transmission model. The study finds that areas most vulnerable to the severe weather are coastal regions, where the high likelihood of hurricane landfalls and increased storm surge potential put the power grid at greatest risk. The power transmission infrastructure is also disproportionately affected, with transmission lines and substations in these areas experiencing higher levels of damage. The results of the study are presented in terms of conditional probability and expected value of damage, providing valuable insights to grid operators and planners.

This paper confirms the three balls conjecture for functions u subject to certain conditions related to Dirac operators in n-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we prove that if u is a harmonic function within the ball B(0,1), with u restricted to the surface of the unit ball having zero n-th root, and u's first derivative bounded within the ball, then u must be identically zero.

We investigate the phase-space dynamics of the heterochaos system under its Baker map representation, particularly its behavior on the boundary of a fundamental domain. This investigation links the system's mixing properties to the geometric structure of its map. We also show that the system's maximal entropy measures align with the survival of a related Dyck system, a symbolic model that exhibits a sudden transition from a solvable to an insolvable problem. This connection enables us to identify a natural mechanism for the breakdown of entropy accessibility in the heterochaos system.

We examine the potential of future high-energy colliders, including the 27 and 100 TeV proton-proton colliders and the LHC with upgraded sensitivity, in detecting expanded scalar sectors. By simulating the production and decay of additional Higgs bosons, we investigate their detectability in various configurations. The study focuses on observing additional scalar particles in final states with four bosons, specifically $bb\gamma\gamma$, $\tau\tau\gamma\gamma$, and $hh$, and final states with four leptons, $l^+l^-\ell^+\ell^-$. The analysis considers multiple production modes of the heavy scalar, including $gg$, $b\bar{b}$, and $W^+W^-$, to determine the optimal production mechanisms and the required production rates for detection at future colliders.

This paper introduces a new generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet that builds upon the WaveNet architecture, incorporating an expanded convolution neural network to model pitch-dependent spectral correlations. The proposed method demonstrates improved efficiency in modeling periodic structures and spectral correlations, resulting in a more effective autoregressive raw waveform model. The results of our experiments, conducted using the LJSpeech dataset, show that Quasi-Periodic WaveNet achieves a lower loss per frame and a higher likelihood per sample compared to the standard WaveNet architecture.

To address the challenges of preference sparsity and subjectivity, a novel approach called BiPRC is proposed, which utilizes item-specific biclustering to capture individual user preferences in an unsupervised manner. BiPRC incorporates a user-oriented clustering method that groups users based on their shared preferences for specific items, and subsequently models each bicluster's rating behavior using a regression analysis. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets, which showcase BiPRC's ability to outperform state-of-the-art recommender systems while maintaining computational efficiency.

The presence of various stellar activity indicators provides essential information for determining the characteristics of a star's activity cycles. This study utilizes high-cadence observations from the HARPS-N solar telescope, spanning 2013-2019, to analyze the relationship between different activity indicators and the star's oscillations. The observed relationships between these indicators and oscillations are then used to create a model, which is used to predict the correlations for periods and amplitudes of oscillations that have not been observed before. The results of this study match the patterns seen in other stars, and the study also explores new activity indicators that could be used in the future.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from a Majorana and those from other non-Majorana topological superconducting states, we suggest utilizing a technique that incorporates resistive electrodes in tunneling spectroscopy. This involves measuring the local density of states within a hybrid nanowire/electron gas system under the influence of an ohmic dissipation channel. The presence of this channel causes Ohmic dissipation, which affects tunneling currents in a way that differs for Majorana and non-Majorana states, leading to distinct dissipations effects observable in tunneling spectra. The proposed approach enables the identification of a Majorana zero-energy peak through a noticeable asymmetry in the real part of the tunneling current's spectral density and a sign change in the imaginary part, whereas non-Majorana states exhibit a decreased asymmetry and no sign change. The effectiveness of this method is validated through numerical simulations under realistic conditions of disorder in nanowires.

The theory of shadows in higher category serves as a useful tool for analyzing the properties of bicategories that lack invertible morphisms. By leveraging the concept of shadows, we are able to derive a precise characterization of the extension of the fundamental bicategory of a point, which corresponds to the category of 1-dimensional bordisms. Additionally, the concept of shadows allows us to prove that the category of extended bordisms, which corresponds to the fundamental homotopy type of a point, is characterized by the absence of invertible morphisms and exhibits a distinct homotopy type.

We are addressing the challenge of applying style transfer techniques to color images, specifically by establishing a connection between pairs of images that differ only in hue. To achieve this, we have developed a neural network that can learn a mapping between the two hues, and even reverse this mapping, using a distillation process that combines supervision with self-supervision. The key to our model's success lies in its ability to leverage internal contradictions within paired images, and also to utilize external image collections that are readily available. The efficacy of our model is demonstrated through a range of qualitative and quantitative evaluations on diverse datasets, including natural scenes, artistic images, and medical images.

This technical report summarizes the winning methods employed by the authors' team, "Lover's Wish", in the CVPR 2022 AQTC competition. The team's approach involved utilizing a transformer-based model to predict the most accurate answer choice for each question, and a set of predefined rules was also applied to rule out obviously incorrect options and fine-tune the model's predictions. The report also outlines the strategy for question type identification, which was based on the analysis of multiple choice questions within the AlQuran TPP dataset. The team's results demonstrated a 0.73 accuracy level in predicting the best answer choice and a 0.81 accuracy level in identifying the correct question type.

The intricate dance of snowflakes falling through the atmosphere is a complex phenomenon that has captivated scientists for centuries. The diversity of snowflake shapes, ranging from delicate hexagons to intricate patterns, hints at the complex interactions between these crystals and the turbulent air currents that facilitate their settlement. The "sweeping" hypothesis proposes that certain air currents selectively capture slower snowflakes, leaving faster ones behind. This study, conducted in a controlled laboratory setting, provides the first empirical evidence for the sweeping hypothesis by tracking over 10,000 snowflakes under various turbulent conditions. The results reveal that larger snowflakes are indeed more likely to be removed by turbulent eddies, while smaller ones persist in the air for longer periods. The associated timeframes for this process are in line with expectations from established theoretical models.

We've developed a novel approach to robot navigation by combining the processes of
exploring and learning. Unlike traditional methods that focus on either active sensing
or using learned models for prediction, our method simultaneously exploits sensor data
and trains a predictive model, which guides sensor collection through a connection to
prediction uncertainty. The result is a highly efficient strategy for active sensing.
Our approach is demonstrated by achieving significant reductions in sensor measurements
necessary for localization tasks, while also learning high-accuracy models of the world
environment.

In the field of Particle Flow Detectors, the Three-dimensional Sparse Tubular Pixelation (3D-SP) design offers a high detection accuracy for individual particles, but its overall data rate remains high due to a lack of particle direction information, resulting in poor data reduction efficiency. To overcome this limitation, we propose an autoencoder-based method that utilizes a bicephalous structure, where one head maps the data to a directional space and the other head converts it into a lower-dimensional representation. This approach significantly improves the data reduction efficiency of 3D-SP by 2-4 orders of magnitude without compromising reconstruction accuracy.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity model, we've derived the thermodynamic potential of galaxy clusters. From this, we calculated the thermodynamic quantities such as pressure, energy density, and entropy per mass unit. We then applied these calculations to statistically analyze galaxy clusters at different redshifts. Our analysis involved determining the entropy per mass unit and temperature as a function of the average overdensity $\Delta_c$ and redshift $z$. We also derived equations for the average temperature and entropy per mass unit, which we validated with existing data from the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect. We found our theoretical results match the empirical data, suggesting the gravity theorem holds for galaxy clusters.

In this paper, we explore the concept of $f$-vector saturation for convex geometric hypergraphs. We establish a specific upper limit on the number of extreme points in a convex geometric hypergraph of order $n$ with a given $f$-vector. This leads to further findings regarding the extremality of extreme points and the formation of extreme faces in such hypergraphs.

To investigate the angular distribution of alpha particles, a 60 MeV beam of $^{6}$Li was directed at $^{51}$V targets, yielding an $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V reaction. The resulting $^{6}$Li and $^{51}$V targets were positioned in an angular frame within the IGISOL-POSTLIC facility, enabling the detection of alpha particles via a silicon detector. The experiment was conducted at an energy of 60 MeV using $^{6}$Li beam on $^{51}$V targets, and the observed alpha particles exhibited a forward angular distribution. The findings were compared to theoretical models, specifically the Monte Carlo code, EMPIRE, which showed a discrepancy of approximately 10% between the observed and predicted cross-sections.

The Pacific lamprey is an ancient, eel-like fish with a unique ability to move across wet surfaces by contracting its muscles and using its suction cups to propel itself upwards in a crawling motion. This study aimed to understand the Pacific lamprey's behavior and apply the insights to develop a robot inspired by its movements. Researchers observed Pacific lamprey in the wild to identify the key movements involved in its locomotion, which was then simulated using a physical robot to verify the results and inform future robotic designs.

A novel approach to colon-cancer treatment is developed through an individualized therapy model, built upon a Fokker-Planck framework. This method incorporates the dynamics of the immune system's response to colon-cancer evolution, modeled as a multi-population genetic variation process. An optimal treatment strategy is identified by maximizing the probability of a successful immune response over a range of possible treatment cycles. A second-best solution is also defined as a fallback option if the optimal treatment is not feasible. Case studies demonstrate the method's ability to identify the most effective treatment cycles for a patient based on their unique medical history.

This study introduces a novel wireless D2D communication framework that enables devices to share information through direct, mesh networking, and investigates the Age of Information (AoI) optimization of this mesh network's topology via a deep learning approach. To maintain network efficiency, the D2D transmission layer is managed by a centralized planner that reconfigures the network by turning D2D mode on or off for individual devices. The planner's objective is to minimize the average AoI and balance network load while adhering to D2D transmission regulations. Given the intricate relationship between network topology and AoI, direct optimization is impractical, thus we propose a deep learning solution that leverages a planner with a neural network architecture capable of learning to configure the D2D network by observing the results of its actions.

This study analytically demonstrates the preservation of helicity in a perfect fluid, described by the compressible Euler equations, for any smooth initial conditions. In the special case of incompressible fluids, this finding reaffirms previous research.

We have found a hidden symmetry in the reflection coefficient for the Davey-Stewartson II equations, which arises from a specific type of long-wave approximation. This symmetry explains why the reflection coefficient often exhibits a large value for certain wave number directions.

In-depth analysis of binary black hole systems detected through gravitational waves reveals that many inspiraling paths exhibit small eccentricities, which are typically assumed to be negligible. However, for detections that approach the threshold of LIGO-Virgo, higher eccentricities become more plausible, potentially influencing the accuracy of gravitational wave data interpretation. To better understand this, we used post-Newtonian theory to model the remnants' final orbits and their residual eccentricities. Our results show that for all masses ratios, the eccentricity distribution peaks at or below 0.05, and the probability of exceeding 0.1 is less than 0.1% for all masses ratios. Additionally, we found that the eccentricity probability thresholds are inversely related to the masses ratio, and that the inspiraling path's characteristics prior to the final orbit have little impact on its residual eccentricity.

A novel X-ray amplifier design is proposed, which builds on the principle of a free-electron laser oscillator. By incorporating a long, thin gas target for ionizing and emitting ions, the oscillator's feedback loop is disrupted, enabling the ions to serve as a pump for a downstream gas attenuator, effectively creating an X-ray laser. This concept leverages the natural energy spread of the ions to achieve a high intensity output, bypassing the need for a feedback loop and achieving a high gain of 10^4 with an extremely low energy pulse of 100 nJ at 10 Hz.

This paper addresses the problem of identifying incidents on dynamic graphs, which are networks whose structure changes over time by adding or removing edges and nodes. The incident detection problem on dynamic graphs is a critical issue in various applications such as transportation systems and social network analysis. We propose a novel approach that detects incidents by analyzing changes in node connectivity during the graph's evolution. The method relies on a spatio-temporal graph representation, which enables the identification of incident nodes and the timing of incidents. We evaluate our approach using synthetic data and compare it with existing methods on two transport-related datasets.

The nature of shock waves in a medium with varying density is a complex phenomenon that has been extensively researched. When an initial pressure pulse propagates through such a medium, it generates an inward-moving shock wave that reaches a steady equilibrium, characterized by a constant pressure pulse behind it. This problem has been extensively studied in different density profiles, but a comprehensive solution has yet to be achieved. In this work, we derive a self-consistent solution to this problem for a specific density profile, $r^{-s}$, for which we demonstrate the existence of a steady-state solution, and further, we show that this profile can be achieved asymptotically as time tends to infinity.

The growing presence of Artificial Intelligence systems in everyday life has created a pressing need for their explanations, which can ensure users' trust in these systems. The process of making AI systems understandable to humans is called explainability. Current methods of addressing explainability primarily focus on technical aspects, with little consideration for its social implications and user-centered requirements. This paper explores the potential for Requirement Engineering to contribute to the explainability of AI systems, proposing a user-centered approach to identify and meet the needs of stakeholders involved in explainability.

The classification of colorectal polyps based on histopathological examination is critical for determining the risk of these growths turning into cancer. The process of examining polyp tissue involves analyzing a small sample, typically a whole-mount section, to identify and classify any abnormal cell growth patterns. The traditional method of examining these samples is a labor-intensive, time-consuming process that requires significant expertise. To aid in the development of more accurate and efficient polyp classification methods, we have created the UniToPatho dataset, a comprehensive collection of 2000 histopathological images, each measuring 7000x, along with detailed annotations that outline the areas of cell abnormality. The dataset also includes 80 images from 10 whole-mount histopathological samples, providing a more extensive understanding of the cell patterns. The UniToPatho dataset is available for public use at the link https://zenodo.org/record/5116545.

Data leakage in zero-error source coding occurs when a covert sender transmits classified information to an unsuspecting receiver through an unreliable channel. This process happens without the original sender being aware of it, and is undetectable by the receiver who may not even utilize the channel. A new framework for analyzing data leakage in zero-error source coding has been developed using graph theory, and is applied to previously existing models of data leakage.

Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging technology allows for effective remote sensing in various applications by utilizing radar waves. However, the SAR raw data is heavily affected by noise, which necessitates processing through a series of nonlinear operations like speckle removal and focusing. This paper presents a novel deep generative model, MrSARP, that integrates a hierarchical prior to enhance noisy SAR raw data. The integrated framework leverages a stacked bidirectional autoencoder to capture high-level correlations in SAR data and a convolutional neural network to extract dense features. The generative model is then optimized using a stochastic gradient variational Bayes method to produce samples, which serve as a prior for SAR image reconstruction. The framework's performance is evaluated on multiple SAR datasets, which demonstrates its superiority over existing methods in terms of image quality and the number of modes produced.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant incorporates a hybrid strategy that combines quantum circuits with classical spin-down problems. The QAOA method's performance relies on optimizing the QAOA parameters, angle $\alpha$ and $\beta$. We've developed a Bayesian tuning approach to automatically optimize these parameters, angle $\alpha$ and $\beta$, without the need for extensive grid searches. The proposed method is tested on MAX-3-XOR and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models, yielding improved results compared to existing methods.

This project involves developing a program that can calculate the overlap area between two ellipses. The algorithm used will be explained in detail, along with any challenges encountered and how they were overcome.

Building upon existing research into continuous duration reasoning, we have adapted the q-learning algorithm to function in continuous durations. This involved formulating a dynamic environment where an agent navigates a plane with a time component, using a policy guided by a temporal logic formula. We have demonstrated that our environment can be learned through a temporal model, and successfully applied our adaptation of q-learning within it.

Using an advanced computational method, we've studied the magnetic properties of a complex triangular-lattice Hubbard model, which exhibits complex magnetic phases. We've discovered that the ground state of this system is a long-range ordered 120-degree state, which can be explained using a theoretical concept called order-by-disorder. We've also found that at a certain intermediate coupling strength, the system undergoes a transition from a 120-degree order to a quantum spin glass phase as the coupling strength increases. We've developed a mean-field theory on the phase diagram and the results show that the spin glass phase persists up to a strong coupling limit. We've compared our results with existing experimental and theoretical data and found that the obtained phase diagram is consistent with experimental results obtained through neutron scattering experiments.

A novel spine localization and identification method is proposed in this paper, designed to function effectively on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scans. The proposed technique employs a straightforward and efficient spinal column alignment process to facilitate accurate identification of vertebral bodies. A mathematical optimization method is then used to determine the positions of vertebral bodies, constrained by anatomical rules to prevent unrealistic solutions. The technique was validated using 348 CT scans and 160 MRI scans, and was found to be a reliable method for localizing vertebral bodies. The proposed method was compared with a state-of-the-art commercial software, and was found to be a reliable and efficient alternative.

This paper explores the fluctuating dynamics of currents in stochastic thermodynamics, focusing on their inherent gauge invariance. We establish that this invariance allows for the determination of a unique, gauge-independent average limit that applies to any stationary or quasi-stationary process. This average limit can be calculated as the average of the current's limiting value, normalized by its standard deviation. We also derive the average limit for the entropy production rate and confirm that it satisfies the non-negative divergence condition, as required by the second law of thermodynamics.

We have developed a method to study changes in relative quantum geometry to the first order in a specific mathematical context. This involves examining how relative quantum geometry adapts when a given algebraic variety undergoes a specific type of mathematical transformation. Our approach relies on an initial condition in which the variety changes are gradual and can be broken down into smaller, manageable components. Building on existing research by Berman and Ma-Marsoof-Sebbar, we have extended their findings to a broader mathematical scenario. Specifically, we have applied our methods to examine the impact of mathematical variety changes on relative quantum geometry in the cases of cubic surfaces and hypersurfaces of higher degree.

We theoretically and experimentally investigate the phenomenon of complete acoustic wave transmission between two piezoelectric crystals under mechanical and electrical resonance. The condition for achieving this transmission requires the crystals' resonance frequencies to be the same, as well as their polarizations being perpendicular to each other. The experiment was successfully conducted using two different combinations of piezoelectric materials: lead zirconate titanate (PZT) and quartz, demonstrating the complete transmission of acoustic waves. The experiment's findings were accurately predicted by the developed theoretical model.

We suggest a reservoir of light that is derived from exciton-polariton condensates in microcavity systems, which can be manipulated by external coherent and incoherent stimuli. The interplay between the stimulated emission and spontaneous scattering of light leads to the formation of a non-equilibrium reservoir with distinct spectral and spatial characteristics. This reservoir can be used to study the long-term effects of photon-photon interactions and to develop new optical processes, such as all-optical modulation and switching.

The exoplanet transiting system K2-22 bears a unique characteristic: the bright planet K2-22 b periodically alters its brightness due to large-scale atmospheric phenomena. These changes are most pronounced in the near-infrared band, particularly at 2.09 microns where a significant decrease in brightness is observed. Our analysis using the Large Binocular Telescope reveals that the planet's atmosphere is likely home to a layer of compacted dust particles, possibly resulting from the interaction between the planet's upper atmosphere and a layer of clouds or the planet's interior. This dust layer is characterized by particles approximately 1-10 microns in diameter. Our findings also indicate a substantial increase in the mass lost by the planet each year, estimated to be around 2.5 billion kilograms. This significant mass loss is likely a result of the planet's close proximity to its host star, causing it to orbit through the star's habitable zone and resulting in the observed changes in brightness.

We establish a coherence property for the Milnor fiber of a polynomial system using a novel approach, which leverages the flatness of its critical locus. This leads to a significant extension of the coherence property for isolated singularities of a single variable, initially proven by Migliore and Sullivant. The proof relies on an algebraic geometric method, which involves analyzing the constancy of topological Euler characteristic along a family of seminormal deformation links.

Daany is an open-source C# library that facilitates data analysis by leveraging popular data science frameworks such as NumPy, SciPy, pandas, and scikit-learn. It enables users to perform various data operations like data frames, linear algebra calculations, and machine learning tasks without the need for additional external dependencies. Daany is designed to be a standalone.NET library that can be used in both Windows and Linux environments, perfect for.NET developers who want to integrate data analysis capabilities into their own projects.

This text explores the Galileo-Clavius affair through the lens of their contrasting views on the role of mathematics in science. While Galileo advocated for a flexible, versatile mathematics that could be adapted to scientific inquiry, Clavius upheld a more rigid, traditional stance. This chapter examines how their disagreement stemmed from distinct perceptions of mathematics and its relationship to the natural world, revealing a deeper historical dynamic that influenced the Scientific Revolution.

The Big Bang Nucleosynthesis model relies on Saha's ionization equation to analyze the universe's composition. However, this study reveals that Saha's equation is not a reliable tool for making precise predictions, as it is based on an incorrect mathematical approach that leads to inaccurate results. Specifically, as the universe's temperature decreases, the predicted abundances of light elements show a significant and unrealistic increase. In contrast, this study develops a new mathematical framework for studying ionization by leveraging non-Gaussian influences and stochastic processes.

The integration of the magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations with the flux-corrected quasi-linear method and the fully-implicit particle-in-cell model reveals a comprehensive simulation tool for complex plasma and magnetic field interactions. This combined model effectively balances accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling detailed simulations of the Sun's corona and other astrophysical environments. A specially developed embedded technique allows for a seamless integration of the MHD and PIC models, which is particularly beneficial for identifying the critical threshold of the Alfvén speed that distinguishes two-fluid and MHD behaviors. Furthermore, detailed analysis of magnetic reconnection and island coalescence in various scenarios demonstrates the capability of this model to provide in-depth insights into these complex astrophysical phenomena.

Amanuensis is a novel computer program designed to assist novice programmers in the educational process. Unlike other systems, Amanuensis does not simply provide a drill-and-practice regimen of solved examples; instead, it serves as a tutor and study companion. By leveraging the strengths of modern computer technology, Amanuensis offers an enriched learning experience that is not feasible for human tutors to replicate. The program is comprised of two primary components: a sophisticated knowledge base and a range of innovative teaching tools. The knowledge base is constructed from a detailed description of the programming skills, along with a model of the learning process, while the teaching tools are designed to facilitate various instructional methods. The program's capabilities are exemplified through a case study of a high school computer science curriculum.
